client: I've been really struggling lately with taking care of my mom — she was diagnosed with Alzheimer's last year and it feels like every week she needs more from me. I'm exhausted all the time, and I feel this constant guilt like I'm never doing enough, even when I'm giving everything I have. Honestly, I'm not sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the situation isn't going to change.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds incredibly heavy — the exhaustion, the guilt, the grief of watching your mom change, all at once. I notice that even as you're describing all of this, there's something in how you're speaking that feels almost... quietly resigned, like part of you has already withdrawn a little, maybe to protect yourself. I'm wondering if underneath the doubt about whether talking will help, there might also be a kind of weariness about being truly *heard* — and I'd really like this to be a space where that can happen.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah... I think you're right that I've kind of checked out a little. therapist: That kind of protective skepticism makes complete sense — when you've felt unseen for so long, hoping again feels risky, almost not worth the effort. I want you to know I'm not here to hand you a quick fix or a checklist, because what you're describing — this slow, ambiguous loss of someone who's still right in front of you — deserves so much more than that. Can you tell me a little more about what "getting it" would actually look like for you, what it would feel like if someone truly understood?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, I'm not even sure I know what that would look like anymore. I think it would feel like someone not rushing to reassure me or tell me to "focus on the good days," but just... sitting with how strange and sad it is that my mom is still here but also kind of not. Like, I just want someone to acknowledge that I'm grieving something that doesn't have a name yet, and that it's okay to feel lost about it.
therapist: What you just described — grieving someone who is still here, for a loss that doesn't have a word yet — that is real, and it's one of the loneliest kinds of pain there is, and I don't want to move past it. I hear you: you're not looking to be cheered up or redirected, you're looking for someone to just sit in that strange, sad in-between place with you, and I can do that. You're not lost because you're doing something wrong — you're lost because you're in territory that's genuinely disorienting, and that makes all the sense in the world.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Thank you for saying that. I think that's the first time I've felt like someone actually got it, instead of trying to hand me a solution or tell me to focus on the good memories. It's just... really hard to sit with the fact that my dad is still here, but the person I knew, the one who remembered my name and laughed at my jokes, he's mostly gone now.
therapist: It means a lot that something landed, and I want to gently stay with what you just shared — I noticed you've been talking about your mom, and just now you said your dad. And whatever the answer, what you're describing — that specific loss of being *known* by your parent, of being the person they laughed with — that's such a tender, particular kind of heartbreak.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

therapist: That image of still being able to hear his laugh but feeling like you'll never *make* it happen again — that's such a precise and painful way to describe what you're living with. I'm wondering if your dad's laugh meant something even more particular because of that — like he was the one who really *saw* you.

client: Yeah... I think that's probably true, even though it's hard to say out loud. He was the one who would notice when something was off with me, without me having to explain it — my mom was always kind of checked out, like she was there physically but somewhere else entirely. So when he died, it wasn't just losing him, it was like losing the only person who actually knew who I was.
therapist: Losing him wasn't just losing a person — it was losing the one relationship where you didn't have to work to be seen, where you could just *be* known, and that's an enormous thing to carry. The way you said that just now was so quiet and careful, like you're holding something very fragile, and I want you to know you don't have to protect yourself from the weight of it here. I'm sitting with you in this — what's it like to say that out loud, maybe for the first time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It's... strange, actually. But you said something about not having to work to be seen, and that landed somewhere deep, because I don't think I've let myself admit how exhausting it is to feel invisible to everyone else now.
therapist: What you just described — keeping things vague on purpose as a way of managing the pain — that's not avoidance in a shameful sense, it's actually something you've been doing to survive, and it makes complete sense. And yet something in how you're speaking right now feels like it's moving fast, like part of you is rushing a little, maybe because sitting still with this newly-named thing feels almost too exposed. I want to slow down with you here — you said feeling invisible to everyone else is exhausting, and I'm wondering what it's been costing you, day to day, to keep carrying that alone.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, you're right that I was kind of speeding through it, and I didn't even notice until you said that. It's like if I keep moving, I don't have to actually feel how heavy it is. The cost of it... I guess I'm always tired, like bone-tired, because I'm constantly performing this version of myself that seems fine, seems connected, when really I go home at the end of the day and there's just this silence that feels louder than anything.
therapist: That image of silence that feels louder than anything — I think that's one of the most honest things you've said today, and it takes courage to name it. There's something that strikes me about how you described it though — your words are carrying something heavy, but your voice got very soft and quick, almost like you were skimming over the surface of something vast. I'm wondering if that silence at the end of the day is the moment when the performance finally stops — and what it's like to just be alone with yourself in it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I think you're right that I was skimming over it — I do that a lot, actually, just kind of rush past the parts that feel too big to look at directly. And when you say "the performance finally stops," that landed somewhere uncomfortable because I think that's exactly it — like all day I'm managing how I come across to people, and then at night there's just... me, and I'm not sure I actually like that person very much. It's easier to stay busy, to stay useful to someone, than to sit in that quiet and feel how empty it gets.
therapist: What you just said — that you're not sure you like that person, the one who's there when the busyness stops — that's such an important and brave thing to name, and I don't want to rush past it either. I'm curious about that person you meet in the quiet: is it that you don't like who you are, or is it more that being alone with yourself means being alone with everything you've lost, and that feels unbearable? Because those are very different things, and I think it matters which one it is.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech
